reasoning: 1. TARGET ENGAGEMENT: No biomarker data available to assess whether nilotinib engaged BCR-ABL. However, nilotinib is a well-established BCR-ABL inhibitor with known pharmacology, so target engagement is likely but unconfirmed in this trial. 2. PATHWAY MODULATION: No pathway biomarkers reported to assess downstream biology changes. 3. CLINICAL TRANSLATION: Primary endpoint clearly failed - 4-month PFS rate was only 27% in no CNS mets cohort and 12.5% in CNS mets cohort, both well below typical efficacy thresholds. PFS was also short at 3.4 and 2.4 months respectively. Only 2 partial responses achieved in the better-performing cohort. 4. POPULATION EFFECTS: Clear difference between CNS and non-CNS metastatic cohorts, with non-CNS performing better (27% vs 12.5% 4-month PFS rate, 3.4 vs 2.4 months median PFS). However, both subgroups failed to meet efficacy thresholds. 5. CONFOUNDERS: Small sample size (N=20) suggests underpowered study. Single-arm design with no control makes interpretation difficult. The rationale for using a BCR-ABL inhibitor in melanoma (which typically lacks BCR-ABL mutations) appears weak, suggesting wrong population/mechanism mismatch.

failure_modes.evidence: Nilotinib targets BCR-ABL, which is characteristic of CML/ALL, not melanoma. The trial enrolled melanoma patients without apparent BCR-ABL mutations, representing a fundamental mechanism-population mismatch.
Sample size of only 20 patients is very small for detecting meaningful efficacy signals, especially in a single-arm design without historical controls.
